Hi! I'm an aspiring engineer from India, passionate about space exploration, satellite technology, AI, programming, and scientific innovation. I have experience working on independent projects involving Earth observation, satellite simulations, and software development. I'm continuously improving my skills in Python, C++, and web development.

Our team, QUANTUM CLUSTER, is working on FIRETRACE, a project focused on harmonizing NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire data.
summary:
FIRETRACE is an open-source web application that turns NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) into one harmonized burning-activity calendar for any area on Earth.

The challenge is that the sensors count fires differently. VIIRS’s 375 m pixels detect about 7 times more fires than MODIS’s 1 km pixels, so simply joining the records creates a false jump in 2012. FIRETRACE places every detection on an equal-area 1 km grid and learns a conversion factor for each satellite and area from the years when both were observing. It then tests that factor on held-out years. Each month in the calendar shows which satellite it came from, the factor used and its uncertainty. Factors that fail validation are rejected, not used, and months without data are shown as missing, never as zero.

We validated it on 10.7 million real detections for India from 2000 to 2026. It reproduces the March–April peak and Punjab’s November crop-burning season, including its decline since 2021.

This matters because governments, researchers and communities need a long, consistent and honest fire record to track burning, test policies and protect air quality.
details:
What it does and how it works

FIRETRACE is a web app that turns NASA FIRMS fire detections from the MODIS satellites (Terra and Aqua, since 2000) and the VIIRS satellites (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, since 2012) into one harmonized burning-activity calendar for any place on Earth.

You choose an area on the map. It can be a box, a country, or a point with a radius, for example 100 km around a city. FIRETRACE then shows month by month how much burning happened there over the years.

The tricky part is that the two sensor types don’t see fires the same way. VIIRS has sharper pixels, so over India it records about seven times more fires than MODIS. Joining the two records directly would show a fake jump in 2012.

FIRETRACE works in four steps:

  1. It imports the NASA files and checks every row.
  2. It places each detection on an equal-area 1 km grid.
  3. For each area, it learns how the satellites’ counts relate during the years when both were working, and it tests that relationship on years it never saw.
  4. It shows the result as a calendar, charts and a map, which you can download as images or CSV.

Every month shows which satellite it came from and how uncertain it is. If a conversion fails its test, it isn’t used. Missing data is shown as missing, never as zero.

Benefits and intended impact

It gives a long, consistent fire record that people can trust:

  • Forest departments and governments can see when burning seasons happen and whether policies, like crop-burning bans, are working.
  • Researchers and students get a clean 26-year series with uncertainty.
  • Journalists and citizens can check their own area in seconds.

We tested it on about 10.7 million real detections for India from 2000 to 2026. It clearly shows the March–April fire season and Punjab’s November crop burning, which has dropped sharply since 2021.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, pandas, Parquet files and SQLite.
  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet for maps, and Recharts for charts.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS archive downloads and the FIRMS API.
  • Testing: 270 automated tests (pytest and Vitest).
  • Code: on GitHub under the MIT license.
  • AI assistance: we used Claude, an AI coding assistant, to help write code and documentation. Our team made the design decisions, ran and tested everything on real NASA data, and checked the results.
  • Hardware: runs on a normal laptop. We kept memory use under about 0.6 GB even for 26 years of data.

What makes it creative

Most fire tools show one sensor at a time or simply add the sensors together. FIRETRACE harmonizes them for each area separately and is open about how good the conversion is. Each calendar cell carries its own source and uncertainty. The tool also rejects its own conversions when they fail validation, as Terra’s did over Punjab.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: we never fake data, never show missing months as zero, and never mix sensors without converting them.
  • Different launch dates: each satellite started at a different time, and their overpass times differ.
  • Global coverage: it works for any area on Earth.
  • Performance: it runs on an ordinary laptop.
  • Security: API keys are never stored in the code.
  • Accessibility: colours chosen for people with colour-vision deficiency.
  • Credit: proper acknowledgment of NASA’s data.
